confirmed: Source version and scope: the on-file PDF is the six-page E&PDE 2024 conference paper headed 26th International Conference on Engineering and Product Design Education, 5-6 September 2024, Aston University, with footer EPDE2024/1271. The title and four authors match the form. The whole markdown conversion and all six PDF pages were read, through the references; no appendix or supplement is mentioned (PDF pp. 1-6).

Only one empirical comparison is reported: two product-development class sections at Brigham Young University, taught one week apart, with one analogue section and one ChatGPT-assisted section. No random assignment of students, teams, classes, or condition order is reported. The form's quasi_people design and observational context are supported; this paper does not document a randomized people study (PDF p. 2, Section 2; pp. 1-6).

Counts: 35 students participated; analogue had 16 students in four teams of four, and ChatGPT had 19 students in three teams of five and one team of four. Table 1 uses those same 16 and 19 denominators for the output analysis. These are people, not numbers of ideas or ratings; n_randomized must remain null, and the analyzed sample is below 50 (PDF p. 2, Section 2.1; p. 4, Table 1).

The participants were undergraduates from first-year to fourth-year, approximately 75 percent from engineering disciplines. The form's students population and approximate disciplinary description match the methods (PDF p. 2, Section 2.1).

The optional post-workshop survey was completed by 30 of the 35 students, with 15 in each class. Those survey counts concern self-reports and do not replace the output-analysis counts of 16 and 19 (PDF p. 4, Section 3.2 and Tables 1-3).

Intervention and task: ChatGPT version 3.5 supported team associative-thinking ideation through a workstation and shared television display. Teams generated new-product ideas for self-identified problems and recorded sketches and text on Post-it notes (PDF p. 2, Sections 2 and 2.2; p. 3, continuation of Section 2.2.2).

Durations match: a single seven-hour class day; two 8-minute ideation sessions; a 2.5-minute instructional video for each associative-thinking technique; and two additional 1.5-minute ChatGPT videos for the assisted class (PDF p. 2, Sections 2 and 2.2.1-2.2.2).

All three listed outcomes are scored on produced ideas: two product-development instructors counted ideas, affinity-mapped idea groups, and novel, unexpected, or unique ideas. Table 1 aggregates team results by class and reports them per student, supporting the form's set unit. Flexibility is within-team category variety, not a comparison of similarity across different people's outputs (PDF p. 3, Section 2.3.1; p. 4, Section 3.1 and Table 1).

S1-O1 reported string verified: fluency is Analogue (n = 16) 5.6 and ChatGPT (n = 19) 5.1 ideas per student. No SD, test statistic, or p-value is reported (PDF p. 4, Table 1; scoring method p. 3, Section 2.3.1).

S1-O2 reported string verified: flexibility is Analogue (n = 16) 2.8 and ChatGPT (n = 19) 2.6 idea groups per student. No SD, test statistic, or p-value is reported (PDF p. 4, Table 1; affinity-mapping method p. 3, Section 2.3.1).

S1-O3 reported string verified: originality is Analogue (n = 16) 0.8 and ChatGPT (n = 19) 0.4 original ideas per student. No SD, test statistic, or p-value is reported (PDF p. 4, Table 1; definition and instructor scoring p. 3, Section 2.3.1).

The one-line finding accurately states the Table 1 values, the 35-student sample, and the descriptive halving of original ideas per student in the ChatGPT class. The prose also says that analogue students produced twice the number of original ideas on average; no significance test accompanies this comparison (PDF p. 4, Table 1 and Section 4.1).
The form's count of 60 ChatGPT prompts across the two ideation sessions is explicitly printed (PDF p. 5, Section 4.3; prompt categories and counts in p. 4, Table 4).

Core eligibility remains no: the analyzed sample is below 50 and random assignment is not documented, while the outcome-scored-on-output criterion is met (PDF p. 2, Sections 2-2.1; p. 3, Section 2.3.1; p. 4, Table 1; codebook Section 3).

This is an original pilot study, not a review or meta-analysis. Section 2.3, titled Synthesis, describes scoring and summarizing this study's own outputs and surveys; it supplies no pooled cross-study estimate, so the empty synthesis fields are appropriate (PDF pp. 2-4, Sections 2-3).
summary: The 35-student class comparison reports no random assignment, and all three outcome contrasts match the PDF. Unfilled coding fields and omitted idea exclusions require correction; the observational, non-core classification stands.
